title: Restoration: open L6
points: Use the six-node classroom graph. Keep the faulted branch unavailable.
Your task: compare total restored load with service to critical loads.
note: This six-node graph is separate from the voltage feeder. It represents active-power transport, not AC power flow or a time-ordered field switching procedure. Loads are picked up as whole blocks.
caption: Teaching diagram of the model or check used at this notebook step.

title: Read the objective before choosing a plan
points: The priority plan weights two critical loads more heavily.
The baseline maximizes total kW with the same graph, capacities and pickup rules.
note: Critical demand totals 90 kW: 60 kW at node 2 and 30 kW at node 5. The objective expresses a service policy. The difference between the plans comes from that objective. Neither numerical optimizer needs a language model to solve this declared problem.
caption: Teaching diagram of the model or check used at this notebook step.

title: Run L6: sweep the tie capacity
points: Run the whole L6 cell. It solves each capacity and checks the priority MILP by enumeration.
Read served_kw, critical_kw and MILP_matches_exhaustive_check.
note: Start with capacities of 40, 60, 80, 100 and 120 kW. The solver enforces active-power balance, capacity limits, source connectivity, radiality and fault exclusion. Independent enumeration checks the priority objective on this small graph. Agreement supports this formulation; it does not check omitted AC physics.

title: Read the two service plots together
points: Left: total served kW. Right: critical served kW.
Coincident markers mean equal outcomes at that sampled capacity.
note: The markers show sampled capacities rather than a continuous ramp between whole-load pickup plans. A higher capacity may still be too small to add another complete load block. Read both total and critical service before choosing the policy that matches the request.
caption: Actual executed notebook output; source cell classroom-018. Fresh numerical calculation unless explicitly marked archived.

title: Explain the 40 kW tradeoff
points: Priority objective: 130 kW total, including 90 kW critical.
Maximum-total-kW objective: 140 kW total, including only 30 kW critical.
note: Compare the first two output rows, where tie_capacity_kw=40. The priority plan serves 10 kW less total demand while preserving 60 kW more critical demand. These results compare two service objectives, not AI with no AI.
caption: Actual executed notebook output; source cell classroom-018. Fresh numerical calculation unless explicitly marked archived.

title: How Python checks the plan
points: Check available source paths, capacities, balance and the faulted branch.
Then compare the MILP objective with the independent exhaustive check.
note: Numerical verification and evidence binding answer different questions. A correctly bound record may still omit AC voltage, reactive-power or protection constraints. Minimizing energized branches does not calculate the number or order of physical switching operations.
caption: Teaching diagram of the model or check used at this notebook step.

title: Exercise 2: add more tie capacity
points: Append 180. to CAPACITIES_KW, keeping 40. as the first entry. Predict, then rerun L6.
Compare total and critical service at 40 and 180 kW.
At which of these settings do the two objectives agree?
note: Allow one minute to predict, two minutes to edit and run, and one minute to report. At 180 kW, both methods serve 250 kW total and 90 kW critical demand. Keep 40 kW first in the list because L7 binds the first result to the first capacity. Do not reorder the list for this exercise.

title: Debrief: enough capacity removes this tradeoff
points: At 180 kW, both methods serve 250 kW total and 90 kW critical.
The priority policy matters under constrained capacity; it does not improve every setting.
note: Compare the 180 kW result with the 40 kW case before generalizing. Equal service at 180 kW follows from this small graph and its demands; it is not a universal threshold. A single success percentage would hide the service-policy question.

title: Reset the sweep; then run L7
points: Restore the original CAPACITIES_KW list and rerun L6 before L7.
L7 binds the first 40 kW plan, then changes the request to 20 kW.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L7; cell classroom-021; request/evidence binding.
note: Keeping 40 kW first already preserves the L7 example. Resetting the list also makes the saved notebook easy to compare with the default. L7 changes the request capacity and revision without solving a new case. It tests whether the old evidence can still be used.

title: Read the changed-evidence test
points: Original contract: True. Changed rating with old evidence: False.
The stated next step is HOLD the old recommendation and request a fresh solve.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L7; cell classroom-021; request/evidence binding.
note: This output reports evidence binding, not physical infeasibility. A separate fresh solve at 20 kW still gives the 130 kW total and 90 kW critical priority outcome on this graph. L7 itself does not run that solve. Replace the stale evidence because it belongs to a different request, even when the old plan might remain feasible.
caption: Actual executed notebook output; source cell classroom-021. Fresh numerical calculation unless explicitly marked archived.

title: A failed binding asks for a new check
points: “The old evidence is stale” and “the new case is infeasible” are different claims.
Update the request, solve the changed case, verify it and bind the new evidence.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L7; cell classroom-021; request/evidence binding.
note: The diagram's extra topology labels are teaching illustrations. The runnable L7 example changes only the request capacity and revision. Do not say that participants changed topology in the notebook. Ask which numerical step would establish feasibility for the changed request.
caption: Teaching diagram of the model or check used at this notebook step.

title: The agent must preserve the service policy
points: The operator specifies the objective and constraints; the MILP returns the pickup plan.
The agent can request the right solve and explain its tradeoff using the returned evidence.
note: A language model must not silently change priority weights or invent pickup values. A different service policy needs an explicit request and a new solve. This classroom supervisor uses ordinary Python. The numerical difference comes from the optimization objective.
caption: Teaching diagram of the model or check used at this notebook step.

title: State what the model leaves out
points: This active-power graph does not certify AC voltage, reactive-power feasibility or protection.
Its energized branches do not define a field switching sequence.
note: State this boundary clearly and briefly. The result is useful within its declared transport formulation. Actual restoration requires the utility's engineering checks, operating procedure and separate authority.

title: Restoration checkpoint: name the next action
points: For the 40 kW request, explain the 130/90 versus 140/30 service tradeoff.
For a changed request, retain HOLD until current evidence is available.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L7; cell classroom-021; request/evidence binding.
note: Ask each pair to give one number and one condition. They should distinguish three decisions: selecting a service policy, checking current evidence and authorizing a physical switching operation.
